body.text: Democrats seized control of the US Congress on November 3, capturing the Senate and House of Representatives in a nationwide rejection of Donald Trump set to put the brakes on the final two years of his presidency. The Democratic landslide will give the opposition power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump’s administration, and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments. The results reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs, and Trump’s war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular President.

Strategists in both parties said Democrats’ sweeping victories were fuelled by strong turnout of party faithful and independent voters who broke their way in both swing states and Republican strongholds. Democrats also adopted a strategy to field a candidate in every race—even those that just months ago appeared to be long shots. Those bets paid off, particularly as Republicans fielded candidates who struggled to overcome Trump’s unpopularity and voter anger over high prices.

Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot. They did, and Republicans paid the price. Early results and exit polls showed an electorate in a sour mood, delivering a strong rebuke of Trump and his agenda as voters expressed deep unhappiness about high prices and the direction of the country.

Many said they feel worse off than two years ago, and nearly 9 in 10 identified the cost of living as a crucial or major factor in their vote, according to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets that included major television networks and the Associated Press.

Trump was elected in 2024 on a promise to arrest high inflation, but his tariffs on foreign goods and war against Iran have worsened the economic situation for many Americans. His response on the campaign trail was to tell Americans to absorb the higher costs even as his popularity sank to record lows.
Key pickups

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers to claim Michigan’s US Senate seat. El-Sayed, a physician who will become the first Muslim US senator, had 51.8 per cent support compared to Rogers at 46.2 per cent, with about 76 per cent of the ballots counted.

The Democrats’ key pickups included former Navy helicopter pilot Rebecca Bennett, who defeated Republican Congressman Tom Kean Jr. in a closely contested New Jersey seat after the incumbent spent months largely out of public view.

State-level contests also featured striking wins for Democrats. Republican Governor Greg Abbott of Texas lost his reelection bid to Democrat Gina Hinojosa. In Ohio, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton defeated Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy. And in Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman to be elected governor of a US state.

Democrats also flipped seats in state legislatures, breaking supermajorities in Indiana and South Carolina and flipping control of the Wisconsin state Senate. Ahead of the election, polling suggested Democrats had made gains with key constituencies that had backed or moved toward Trump in 2024, including rural voters in states like Iowa and Kansas and Latino voters in states like Arizona and Florida.

Throughout 2026, Trump sought to create a more favourable playing field for his party, including pushing GOP-led states to redraw congressional districts in the hope of creating more Republican-leaning seats. But that effort led to a number of Democratic-led states taking similar steps. It was not immediately clear if either side was advantaged.

The president has also repeated baseless claims of widespread election fraud and tried to increase federal government control over voting, including an aggressive push to curb mail-in voting and suing states to try to get voter records, which his Justice Department has continued to pursue despite pushback from the courts.

To fight their electoral headwinds, the GOP had an enormous financial advantage in what was on pace to be the most expensive election ever. Much of their money came from Trump’s super political action committee and from Elon Musk, who spent heavily in Texas to prop up Paxton.

Musk joked on November 4 about Republicans’ defeat in US midterm elections after spending hundreds of millions of dollars to help the party. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” he wrote on X.
Record spending

Total spending for the 2026 midterms soared to a record $11.9 billion, substantially higher than the $8.9 billion racked up in 2022, according to OpenSecrets, a non-partisan authority on spending in US politics. Campaign fundraising and ad buys jumped in the 2026 races, driven by the outside spending of so-called political action committees. Such outside spending, led by Trump’s mega-billionaire ally Elon Musk, favoured Republicans by some $360 million.

But Democratic candidates proved adept at raising their own funds. House and Senate candidates spent an unprecedented $3.7 billion from their campaign warchests, with Democrats outspending Republicans by $800 million, according to OpenSecrets.
Praises Democrats, deflects blame

Trump congratulated Democrats for doing “a good job” after the party inflicted devastating defeats on his Republican allies, winning back both houses of Congress and picking up several governors’ mansions. But the President, in an interview with Fox News early Wednesday morning, didn’t take responsibility for a long night of GOP defeats, including many in what had been considered reliably conservative states.

“No matter how good the President is, you lose,” Trump said, adding that “because of the gasoline price” Americans had failed to see the economic benefits brought about by his presidency. He said that high fuel prices came about because of the war in Iran, and again defended the US military campaign in the Middle East as necessary to prevent the Islamic Republic from obtaining nuclear weapons.

Trump said he could work with a House and Senate run by the opposition “if the Democrats want to work with me”. He also alluded to the considerable clout that a President has with or without allies in control of Congress. “It’s a power of veto,” Trump said. “It’s one of the stronger powers that a President has, and they’ll send over things that are insane, and I’ll veto them. And after a couple of months of vetoes, they’ll call and they’ll say, ‘How do we get this stuff done?’”
Hakeem Jeffries to become first Black House Speaker

The Democrats’ midterm election win puts Hakeem Jeffries in line to become the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives, with the dual challenge of opposing President Trump while bridging the gap between his party’s moderates and its more vocal progressives.

As speaker, Jeffries, representing a New York City congressional district, would preside over a majority that will be sworn in the first week of January, taking the reins from Republicans who controlled the House for the past four years. “Today begins the great American comeback,” Jeffries proclaimed in a victory speech late on November 3 after media outlets projected the likelihood of Democratic majorities in the House and Senate.

He attacked the Trump-led Republican agenda in Congress over the past two years, pledging to pass legislation reversing steep spending cuts—enacted into law on July 4, 2025—to the Medicaid healthcare program for the poor and people with disabilities.
What happens next

Democrats are preparing a legislative offensive against US President Donald Trump after their sweeping midterm victory handed them control of both chambers of Congress and the power to challenge his policies, investigate his administration and block his nominees.

Robert Garcia, the Democrat expected to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee, fired off a blunt election-night message to Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP”. Oregon Senator Ron Wyden was even more concise, posting a single word: "Subpoenas".

With control of committees in both chambers, Democrats can summon officials, demand documents, and hold public hearings, potentially putting Trump and his senior aides under intense scrutiny. Likely subjects include the Trump family’s business and cryptocurrency dealings, government contracts involving billionaire Elon Musk, cuts to federal agencies, immigration enforcement and the conduct of the Iran war.

Democrats have also signalled interest in the handling of files relating to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The administration could resist demands for testimony or documents, triggering court battles. Democrats could pursue Trump’s third impeachment, though party leaders have not committed to doing so. The House needs only a simple majority to impeach, but removing a president requires a two-thirds vote in the Senate—far beyond the party’s numbers.

The Senate majority gives Democrats another powerful lever: control of confirmations. They can block Trump’s judicial and cabinet nominees, including any selection to fill a Supreme Court vacancy, potentially curbing his influence over the courts long after he leaves office. Democratic Senate chairs will also decide which bills and investigations receive committee attention.
(With inputs from agencies)
